A commuter is a person who regularly travels between two places — almost always between their home and their workplace or school — and then travels back again. This back-and-forth trip happens repeatedly, typically every day or several days a week.

Think of it this way: every morning, millions of people wake up, leave their homes, travel to work, and in the evening, travel back home. They do this day after day, week after week. Each one of those people is a commuter.
What Makes Someone a "Commuter" (Not Just a Traveler)?

This is an important distinction. Not every person who travels is a commuter. Three things define a commuter:

  1. Regularity — It happens repeatedly, on a routine basis (daily, weekly, etc.), not just once or occasionally.
  2. A fixed two-point route — They travel between two specific, consistent places: usually home and work/school.
  3. The purpose is non-leisure — They are traveling to get to a job, school, or a regular obligation — not for fun, vacation, or tourism.

A tourist visiting a new city is not a commuter. A businessperson flying to a different country for a one-time meeting is not a commuter. But someone who takes the train to their office every Monday through Friday and returns home every evening? That person is a commuter.

Commuters use all kinds of transportation. The mode of transport does not change whether someone is a commuter or not — what matters is the routine, repetitive nature of the trip. Common ways commuters travel include:

  • By train or metro — Very common in large cities. These people are often called train commuters.
  • By bus — Public buses are widely used for daily commutes.
  • By car — Many people drive themselves to work. A person stuck in traffic on a highway every morning is a classic commuter.
  • By bicycle — Some people cycle to their workplace daily.
  • By ferry or boat — In cities near water, some commuters travel by boat.
  • On foot — Even people who walk to work every day are technically commuters, though this term is used less often for them.

In recent years, with the rise of remote work, there is even the idea of a digital commuter or someone who has a very short commute (from their bedroom to their home office), sometimes called a "commute of zero." However, the traditional meaning still refers to physical travel.

There is no fixed rule, but a commute is generally understood to be a journey of some meaningful distance — often anywhere from a few kilometers to over 100 kilometers. People who live far from their workplace but travel there regularly are called long-distance commuters. In some countries, people even commute between cities — for example, living in one city and working in another, traveling by high-speed train every day.

The time it takes can range from 15 minutes to several hours, depending on the distance and traffic or transit conditions.
The Feeling and Experience of Being a Commuter

Commuting is often associated with being tiring, repetitive, and time-consuming. A commuter typically spends hours each week just getting to and from work. This is why phrases like "commuter traffic," "rush hour," and "commuter stress" are so common — they describe the crowded, busy conditions that commuters face every day, especially in the morning and evening.

On the other hand, some commuters use their travel time productively — reading, listening to podcasts, or resting.

• "She is a daily commuter who takes the 7 a.m. train to downtown every morning."
  • "The new highway is meant to make life easier for commuters traveling from the suburbs."
  • "As a commuter, he spends nearly two hours on the road every day."
  • "The bus service was designed specifically for commuters heading to the business district."
  • "After years of being a commuter, she finally decided to move closer to her office."

• Commute (verb) — The action itself. "She commutes to work by train." It can also be used as a noun: "Her commute takes 45 minutes."
  • Commuting (noun/gerund) — The general activity. "Commuting in this city is exhausting."
  • Commuter belt / commuter zone — The area surrounding a large city where people live but travel into the city for work. These are residential areas popular with commuters.
  • Commuter town — A town whose residents mostly work elsewhere (usually in a nearby big city) and commute daily.
  • Commuter train / commuter bus — Transport services specifically designed for people commuting, often running at high frequency during rush hours.
A commuter is someone who makes a regular, repeated journey — usually daily — between their home and their place of work or study, regardless of how they travel.
